articles.title: The Healey Dell prophecy: the Lady Eleanor who was said to be 'maid, wife and widow in one day'
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the strange Healey Dell story about Eleanor Byron and a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden — what the old printed collectors actually recorded, what local guides now tell visitors, and what survives as verifiable fact.
articles.summary: A short guide to the strange Healey Dell story about Eleanor Byron and a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden — what the old printed collectors actually recorded, what local guides now tell visitors, and what survives as verifiable fact.
articles.body:
Healey Dell’s cleft in the Spodden — the narrow gorge known locally as the Thrutch and the spot tourists call the Fairies’ Chapel — is one of Rochdale borough’s most durable story‑places. The best‑known version of the tale says a local noblewoman, usually called Lady Eleanor (linked by later tellings to the Byron family), visited a fortune‑teller named Mother Bagden; the woman prophesied Eleanor would be a maid, a wife and a widow all in one day, and on her wedding day the bridegroom was killed. That dramatic sequence is recorded in early nineteenth‑century folklore collectors and is the version repeated by the Dell’s modern heritage interpretation. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

The oldest printed witness we can point to is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire, collected and published in the early 1800s; Roby preserves a long, romance‑style narrative set at Healey that includes a miller, a Fairy‑Chapel, a talisman and the fatal wedding night that fulfils the prophecy. Roby’s book is literary folklore: it records what people were telling in his day rather than supplying contemporary medieval documents about the events described. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

Local interpretation and visitor material at Healey Dell — the Heritage Centre and the site’s guides — now knit Roby’s account together with later Victorian retellings (and with local names such as Chadwick and Healey Hall). The Heritage Centre openly treats the story as legend and presents it alongside geology, mill remains and an account of the great flood of 4 July 1838 that altered the Thrutch feature generations later. Those local guides also cite later local antiquarians (for example William Robertson’s regional histories) as sources for the familiar version. In short: the prophecy story is part of the Dell’s storytelling tradition, preserved in printed collections and in modern visitor interpretation, not in contemporary court rolls or parish registers. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

What is documentary fact here, and what is folklore? Verifiable facts: Healey Dell exists as a managed nature reserve and visitor attraction at 121 Dell Road; the valley contains recognisable industrial archaeology (old mill sites, lodges and a prominent Victorian railway viaduct) and a heritage centre with displays and family trails. Rochdale Borough Council provides the site address, facilities and opening information; the viaduct itself is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those are public, documentable features you can still see. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

What cannot be verified in the surviving records is the supernatural machinery of the tale: a Fairy Queen who issued prophecies, a coven turned to stone, or a named medieval Lady Eleanor whose wedding‑night fate is confirmed in a contemporary legal or parish document. The earliest printed accounts that give the prophecy its shape are collectors’ and antiquarian narratives from the nineteenth century; later guidebooks and the Heritage Centre responsibly present them as legend rather than as archival history. If a claim about a medieval event cannot be found in contemporary documents, it belongs to folklore and local tradition rather than to proven local history. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

For readers who want to follow the trace: read Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the early printed tale; visit the Healey Dell Heritage Centre for the site interpretation and the leaflet material that draws the story together; and see the viaduct and river features for the physical reasons people long ago imagined a tiny ‘chapel’ there. The council’s directory entry gives practical details (address, parking, facilities and the fact the park area is open daily). The short, final point is this: the prophecy of Mother Bagden and Lady Eleanor is an old and well‑preserved piece of Lancashire storytelling — entertaining and locally meaningful — but it should be read as folklore, not as a documented historical event.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Celebrates Achievements of Over 200 Cared-for Children at Annual Awards
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council hosted its annual awards ceremony at Matthew Moss High School, recognising the achievements of more than 200 cared-for children with medals and a day of entertainment.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council held its annual awards ceremony on 16 October at Matthew Moss High School, celebrating the achievements of over 200 cared-for children. The event, known as 'Our Big Day', recognised the resilience and determination of young people in care, with hundreds of medals awarded to honour their individual successes.

The council received 273 nominations from carers, teachers, and social workers, highlighting the inspiring journeys of children up to the age of 12. Awards were given for exceptional progress in education, sporting achievements, acts of kindness, and positive attitudes in the face of adversity. The day included a variety of entertainment, such as trampolines, funfair rides, and face painting, allowing families to create joyful memories together.

Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, expressed her pride in the achievements of the children, stating, "They are all exceptional young people and show phenomenal determination to be their very best. This doesn’t go unnoticed by those around them." The event aimed to provide public recognition for the hard work and accomplishments of these young individuals.

Local businesses sponsored the celebration, contributing to the activities and entertainment provided for families. Notable sponsors included A&T Surfacing Ltd, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, and Rochdale Hornets, among others. This community support helped create a memorable day for the children and their families.

articles.title: St Cuthbert's School in Rochdale Evacuated Following Bomb Threat
articles.excerpt: St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale was evacuated and closed on 16 October after receiving a suspected bomb threat. All students and staff were reported safe, and police are investigating the incident.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

13:57, 16 October 2026

St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale was evacuated and closed on 16 October after receiving a suspected bomb threat. All students and staff were reported safe, and police are investigating the incident.

St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale was evacuated and closed on Friday morning, 16 October, after staff received a communication regarding a possible bomb threat. The school, located on Shaw Road, implemented emergency procedures to ensure the safety of all students and staff.

In response to the threat, Greater Manchester Police were called to the scene, and the school entered a lockdown as a precautionary measure. A spokesperson for the school confirmed that all children and staff were safe and accounted for during the incident. The police assessed the situation and indicated that the call was likely a hoax.

The St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, which oversees the school, stated that specialist security operatives would conduct a thorough sweep of the premises to determine if any further action was necessary. Parents and carers were informed that they could collect their children or give permission for them to travel home safely.

The school is expected to reopen as normal on Monday, 19 October, pending the outcome of the police investigation. Authorities have urged the public to refrain from speculation on social media regarding false rumours related to the incident.

articles.title: St Cuthbert’s evacuated as message reassures parents all children and staff are safe
articles.excerpt: St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust says St Cuthbert’s was evacuated following a possible bomb threat. All children and staff are safe; parents can collect pupils.
articles.content_html:
Latest update — St Teresa of Calcutta trust statement

St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, which oversees St Cuthbert’s RC High School, has released a statement saying staff received a communication detailing a possible bomb threat on Friday morning, 16 October.

The trust says emergency services were called, all school buildings were evacuated as a precaution and Greater Manchester Police attended. All children and staff are safe and accounted for, it says.

Parents and carers can now collect their children or give consent for them to travel home, according to the statement. The trust says specialist security operatives will carry out a full sweep of the building this afternoon. It currently expects the school to reopen as normal on Monday 19 October, subject to further updates.

The trust’s account conflicts with some earlier reports circulating about the incident. In particular, it describes rumours of intruders or weapons on school premises as false. Earlier references to a lockdown should be read alongside this latest statement, which describes a precautionary evacuation following a possible bomb threat.

This remains a developing story. Rochdale Daily will continue to update this article with official information as it is released. The earlier updates below are retained for context; the latest trust statement takes precedence where accounts differ.

Trust statement in full:

Earlier this morning (Friday 16 October 2026), staff at St. Cuthbert's RC High School in Rochdale received a communication detailing a possible bomb threat to the premises.

The emergency services were called and all school buildings were evacuated as a precautionary measure.

All children and staff are safe and accounted for, in line with our established procedures.

Greater Manchester Police attended and parents and carers were notified immediately that their children had been removed to a safe distance and there was no threat or danger to anyone present.

We would like to assure everyone within the St Cuthbert’s School community that the safety and wellbeing of our children remains our absolute priority.

Specialist security operatives will conduct a full sweep of the building this afternoon to confirm if any further actions are required.

Currently, the expectation is that the school will be open as normal on Monday 19 October - but further information will be communicated as needed when received.

Parents and carers can now attend the school to collect their children, or provide consent for their children to travel home.

We’d like to thank parents, carers and colleagues for their understanding and co-operation in this matter.

We’d also urge people to avoid speculation on social media - particularly regarding false rumours, such as any referring to intruders or weapons being present on school premises.

More details will be communicated when appropriate, following consultation with GMP and Rochdale Borough Council.

Source: Statement attributed to St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, supplied to Rochdale Daily on 16 October 2026.

Earlier updates — before the trust statement

Developing update — councillor requests official briefing

Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short has said he is urgently requesting an update from Rochdale Council and Greater Manchester Police following reports of a lockdown at Saint Cuthbert’s High School. In a statement supplied to Rochdale Daily, he said he first learned of the reports through the Manchester Evening News and had not received an official briefing.

His statement does not establish what prompted the incident. The earlier message shared with Rochdale Daily described a precautionary evacuation and said all children and staff were safe and accounted for.

Councillor Tarrant-Short’s statement in full:

I want to address the reports of a lockdown at Saint Cuthbert’s High School.

First and foremost, my thoughts are with the children, their families and the staff. I understand how frightening this situation will be, particularly for parents waiting for information and reassurance.

I want to be clear: I first became aware of this through the Manchester Evening News. I have not received an official briefing.

I am now urgently requesting an update from Rochdale Council and Greater Manchester Police so I can understand what has happened and what support is being provided to those affected.

Having been through a similar situation myself when Newhouse Academy went into lockdown, I know how distressing that uncertainty can feel. Behind every update are children who may be frightened and families desperate to know their loved ones are safe.

I am asking that communication with families is timely, clear and compassionate, and that support is available for anyone left distressed.

Until there is verified information, I will not speculate about the circumstances. Please follow official updates from the school and police, and avoid sharing rumours.

The immediate priority must be the safety and wellbeing of every child and member of staff.

St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale has been evacuated as a precaution, according to a message to parents and carers shared with Rochdale Daily.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Plans Major Investments and Heritage Restoration
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has announced significant investments in heritage restoration and community services, including plans for Hopwood Hall and Middleton's regeneration projects, aimed at boosting local economy and services.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has outlined a series of major investments aimed at revitalising the borough, with a focus on heritage restoration and community services. In a recent column, Councillor Neil Emmott highlighted the council's commitment to enhancing local infrastructure and supporting residents amid ongoing cost-of-living challenges.

A key development is the council's recent victory in the High Court regarding Hopwood Hall, a historic building in Middleton. The ruling provides clarity on the future of the site, which has seen over £1.6 million invested since 2017 by the council and Historic England. Plans for essential repairs and feasibility studies are underway, with the aim of restoring the hall to serve the community and preserve its historical significance.

In addition to Hopwood Hall, the council is advancing its regeneration plans for Middleton. The acquisition of Middleton Old Grammar School is expected to attract a new tenant by the end of the year, while the long-derelict Warwick Mill is also set for redevelopment, potentially including new housing. Furthermore, the transformation of the Middleton Scout Hut into a community venue is in progress, aimed at providing activities and training for young people.

These initiatives are part of a broader strategy to stimulate economic growth and create jobs across the borough. With banking and post office services returning to Middleton town centre in the new year, local leaders are optimistic about the positive impact these developments will have on the community.

articles.title: High Court Trial Begins Over Ownership of Hopwood Hall
articles.excerpt: A two-day trial in Manchester's High Court will determine the future of Hopwood Hall, as Hopwood DePree seeks to reclaim his ancestral home from Rochdale Council.
articles.content_html:
The High Court in Manchester is currently hearing a two-day trial concerning the ownership of Hopwood Hall, a historic manor house in Rochdale. The case involves Hopwood DePree, a descendant of the family that built the hall in the 1420s, and Rochdale Council, which currently owns the Grade II-listed property.

Mr DePree's legal action follows a lengthy collaboration with the council over the past seven years, during which he aimed to restore the dilapidated site. However, in November 2024, the council ended its exclusivity agreement with him, stating that no commercially viable business model had been presented for the property. This decision has led to the current court proceedings, where Mr DePree argues that the council has reneged on an agreement to transfer ownership after planning permission was granted in 2022.

The Hopwood family owned the hall and surrounding land until 1922, after which it changed hands multiple times and fell into disrepair. The council acquired the property to prevent further deterioration, but the future of the hall remains uncertain as the trial unfolds.

The outcome of this trial could significantly impact the future of Hopwood Hall and its restoration, as well as the local community's connection to this historic site. A ruling is expected to clarify the legal standing of Mr DePree's claims and the council's obligations regarding the property.

articles.excerpt: Eighteen runners from Resilience gym in Rochdale will embark on a 100km run across the Arctic wilderness on January 29, 2027, to raise funds for cancer charities.
articles.content_html:
A local fitness community in Rochdale is gearing up for a challenging 100-kilometre run across the Arctic wilderness of Swedish Lapland, set to take place on January 29, 2027. The event, known as the Ultra 4 Cancer challenge, will see 18 runners from Resilience gym tackle extreme conditions, including temperatures that may plunge to -30°C, over the course of two days.

The initiative is led by Martin Stapleton, founder and head coach of Resilience gym. Stapleton, a Rochdale-born former Royal Marines Commando and professional MMA fighter, has a history of extreme fundraising efforts, including kayaking the length of the Rochdale Canal and running along the River Thames to support Help for Heroes. Joining him on this expedition are assistant coaches Greg Egan and Oliver Roxburgh, the latter of whom has a personal connection to the cause.

The team aims to raise vital funds for four cancer charities, highlighting the importance of community support in tackling such a significant health issue. The challenge not only tests the physical endurance of the participants but also serves to raise awareness and funds for cancer research and support services.

As the date approaches, the runners will be preparing for the harsh conditions they will face, with training sessions likely to intensify. Community members interested in supporting the cause can follow the team's progress and contribute to their fundraising efforts through the Resilience gym's social media channels.

articles.title: Jolly Josh welcomes Rochdale families with inclusive play, music and activity sessions
articles.excerpt: The Castleton charity is reaching out to families caring for children and young people with complex medical needs and physical disabilities, with weekly sessions and bookable activities.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale charity Jolly Josh is reaching out to families caring for children and young people with complex medical needs and physical disabilities, with a programme of inclusive activities and support.

Based at 2 Ensor Mill in Castleton, Rochdale, OL11 2NU, the centre welcomes children and young adults aged from birth to 19.

The charity says finding activities where a child is welcomed, understood and supported can be difficult, and wants more parents, carers, relatives and professionals to know what is available.

Its programme includes music and signing, themed play sessions, an after-school club, a youth group and activities that families can book directly with the centre.

Weekly sessions

Sing And Sign runs every Wednesday from 10.30am to 12.30pm, bringing together music, songs and signing to make communication fun.

Themed Stay And Play takes place every Tuesday and Saturday from 9.30am to 12.30pm. Sessions offer activities, friendship and a different theme each week.

Sensory Touch And Music runs every Thursday from 10am to noon, offering a relaxing sensory session.

The After School Club takes place every Wednesday from 4pm to 7pm, with inclusive activities and a light tea offered for every child.

The Youth Group meets every Thursday from 5pm to 8pm, giving young people a welcoming space to socialise, take part in activities and build friendships.

Activities available to book

Hydrotherapy sessions can be booked for families or with the centre’s Hydro Lead.

Private sound bath sessions are also available by contacting the centre, offering an opportunity to take time out of a busy schedule.

Rebound Therapy provides supported movement and sensory experiences using a trampoline, with sessions bookable through the centre.

How to get in touch

Parents, carers, family members and professionals supporting a child with complex medical needs are invited to contact Jolly Josh to learn more about its sessions.

Call 01706 399141, email sarah@jollyjosh.co.uk or visit https://jollyjosh.co.uk/

The centre asks anyone planning to visit to contact the team first so an appointment can be arranged.

Families can contact the centre to discuss which sessions suit their child and ask about booking, availability and charges.

The charity is also encouraging people to share its appeal with families who may not yet know about the support available.

articles.title: Fireworks distributor with Rochdale premises fined £40,000 as fire service takes enforcement action
articles.excerpt: GMFRS has announced prosecutions over fireworks storage and licensing breaches, including a £40,000 fine for Boom Fireworks, which operates premises in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
A national fireworks distributor operating premises in Rochdale has been fined £40,000 following an investigation by Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service.

GMFRS announced prosecutions involving Boom Fireworks Limited and two Greater Manchester retailers after inspectors uncovered fireworks storage and licensing offences.

According to the fire service, Boom Fireworks operates distribution premises in Cheetham Hill and Rochdale. Its director, Hashum Malik, pleaded guilty to storage offences at Manchester Magistrates’ Court on October 6.

Inspectors discovered higher-risk Hazard Type 3 fireworks being stored contrary to licensing requirements. The stock was detained and removed, and the company received a £40,000 fine, alongside a surcharge and prosecution costs.

Separate cases concerned The Vape Store on Hollins Road in Oldham and Wise Buys on Bury Road in Bolton.

The Oldham shopkeeper received a suspended prison sentence after fireworks were stored and sold despite an expired licence. The Bolton shopkeeper received rehabilitation requirements and a curfew after inspectors found fireworks stored and sold without a valid licence. Courts ordered the seized fireworks destroyed.

What this means for late-night fireworks

For Rochdale residents disturbed by repeated late-night fireworks, the announcement highlights enforcement against businesses supplying and storing explosive products.

However, the prosecutions concern storage and licensing offences. Their effect on fireworks nuisance in individual neighbourhoods has not been established.

The existing rules already prohibit setting off fireworks between 11pm and 7am on most nights. The exceptions are:

Bonfire Night: fireworks may be used until midnight.

New Year’s Eve, Diwali and Chinese New Year: the cut-off is 1am.

Midnight is therefore not the usual permitted finishing time: on ordinary nights, the restriction begins an hour earlier.

How to report persistent problems

Greater Manchester Police says irresponsible fireworks use can harm people and animals, damage property and create a serious fire risk.

Residents experiencing an ongoing problem can report fireworks-related antisocial behaviour through GMP: https://www.gmp.police.uk/advice/advice-and-information/asb/asb/antisocial-behaviour/fireworks/

The force also advises reporting retailers selling adult fireworks to under-18s to Trading Standards.

articles.title: Veterans group calls on Rochdale volunteers to help transform Sea Cadets’ outdoor space
articles.excerpt: Get Together After Serving, now based at Denehurst Café, is appealing for volunteers, tools and a donated skip to support Rochdale Sea Cadets.
articles.content_html:
Get Together After Serving, now based at Denehurst Café, is calling on volunteers and local businesses to support a community clear-up for Rochdale Sea Cadets at Hollingworth Lake.

The group, known as GTAS, has been asked to tackle a heavily overgrown and cluttered outdoor storage area at the TS Frobisher Sea Cadets site.

Organisers hope a team of veterans, supporters and community volunteers can transform the space in one day, clearing vegetation, rubbish and old debris.

“This is what GTAS is all about—getting stuck in, helping our community, and supporting the next generation,” the group said.

When and where

The volunteer day takes place on Saturday, October 17, with volunteers meeting at 10am at Hollingworth Lake Council Car Park, Littleborough, OL15 0AZ.

The team will then head to the TS Frobisher Sea Cadets site together.

How volunteers can help

GTAS is asking for as many volunteers as possible, with jobs including lifting, clearing, cutting back vegetation and keeping the team supplied with brews.

Volunteers are asked to bring whatever suitable equipment they have, including shovels and spades; gardening tools and loppers; trimmers and brush cutters; wheelbarrows; heavy-duty gloves, which organisers describe as essential; and sturdy boots.

Local skip company needed

The group is also urgently appealing to a local waste or skip company willing to donate a skip for a few hours on Saturday, October 24, to help remove the waste.

Businesses able to help, or anyone who knows a company that might support the project, are asked to contact GTAS as soon as possible.

Getting involved

Anyone wishing to volunteer should comment on GTAS’s appeal or send the group a direct message, letting organisers know whether they can attend and which tools they can bring.

Residents are also encouraged to share the appeal to help recruit more volunteers and reach businesses that could lend a hand.

“Together we walk. Together we build. Together we remember.”

articles.title: Future of College Bank Towers Uncertain as Renovation Could Take Over a Decade
articles.excerpt: Housing chiefs have stated that renovating the College Bank tower blocks would displace residents for more than ten years, with no decision yet made on their future.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) has confirmed that no decision has been made regarding the future of the College Bank tower blocks, known locally as the Seven Sisters. However, housing officials have warned that any renovation of the iconic structures would require residents to vacate their homes for over a decade.

The Seven Sisters, which have stood for 61 years, are in urgent need of modernisation. Residents have been advocating for refurbishment rather than demolition, and recently appealed to Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig for support in their campaign. If the renovation proceeds, RBH has indicated that the buildings would not be habitable until the extensive work is completed.

The discussion around the future of College Bank began in 2017 when RBH expressed concerns about the buildings nearing the end of their lifespan. In response, tenants formed the Save the Seven Sisters campaign, hoping that a partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would lead to restoration. However, in September 2024, it was announced that this partnership would not continue, prompting further calls for assistance from local leaders.

In November 2024, a Mayoral Taskforce was established to explore options for the College Bank estate. Following safety surveys conducted in October 2025, RBH declared that the blocks were unsafe for occupancy, necessitating the relocation of residents. As the situation develops, the community awaits clarity on the next steps for the future of their homes.

articles.title: Plans for 45-Home Development in Bamford Face Over 300 Objections
articles.excerpt: More than 300 objections have been lodged against plans to demolish a house in Bamford to make way for a new 45-home development, which is recommended for approval by Rochdale Council.
articles.content_html:
Plans to demolish a house in Bamford to facilitate a new 45-home development have sparked significant local opposition, with over 300 objections submitted to Rochdale Council. The proposal, submitted by Wain Homes, involves the demolition of 58 Greenvale, known as Chadwick Farm Barn, to create access to the new housing development planned for land south of the property.

The proposed development includes 39 homes for market sale, comprising 14 three-bedroom, seven four-bedroom, and 18 five-bedroom houses, along with six homes designated for social housing. The council's planning committee is set to review the application on Thursday, following a deferral in August due to concerns regarding the absence of a comprehensive housing masterplan.

Local residents have raised multiple concerns regarding the development, including the premature release of the site, inadequacies in local infrastructure, highway capacity and road safety issues, as well as potential drainage and flooding problems. Additionally, objections highlight the impact on local ecology and landscape, and the effects on the amenity of existing residents.

The planning application comes in the wake of a revised National Planning Policy Framework aimed at boosting housing supply and economic growth. As the council prepares to make a decision, the significant number of objections may influence the outcome of the proposal.

Work to open up overgrown shrub areas at Jubilee Park in Middleton has entered its second phase, with volunteers and council staff joining forces to improve the grounds.

The Friends of Jubilee Park have been working alongside Rochdale Borough Council’s Environmental Management team, carrying out maintenance that includes caring for the park’s collection of rhododendrons.

The group says the work will encourage healthy new growth over the next couple of seasons, improve views and sight lines, and help visitors feel safer.

Opening up densely planted areas is intended to create a brighter, more welcoming park while supporting the long-term health of its shrubs.

Visitors may notice that some sections look temporarily untidy as the work progresses. The Friends have asked for patience, explaining that the maintenance is intended to bring lasting improvements.

“These improvements will bring lasting benefits for visitors and help Jubilee Park continue to thrive,” the group said.

The Friends describe Jubilee Park as a Gold Medal-winning Green Flag park and thanked visitors for their understanding while volunteers and staff care for the grounds.

The latest work forms part of an ongoing effort to maintain the much-loved Middleton green space for everyone who uses it.

articles.title: Inclusive roundabout and zip line feature in plans for new Falinge Park play area
articles.excerpt: Mayoress Iram Faisal has unveiled plans for new play equipment at Falinge Park, including a wheelchair-accessible roundabout, an inclusive seesaw and a double cableway zip line.
articles.content_html:
Plans for a new play area at Falinge Park have been unveiled, with wheelchair-accessible equipment among the attractions proposed for children and families.

Mayoress Iram Faisal shared details of the project, describing it as a deeply personal undertaking in the park where she played as a child.

The proposed equipment includes a double cableway zip line with ramps; a toddler multi-play unit; toddler and junior swings; an inclusive seesaw; a Crazy Gander springer; and a wheelchair-accessible roundabout.

In her announcement, Mrs Faisal said inclusivity had been central to the vision, with the aim of helping more children enjoy the park together.

“Every child deserves the opportunity to play, explore and enjoy their childhood,” she said.

For the Mayoress, the plans also carry memories of her own upbringing.

“Having lived here and played in this very park myself, to now be in a position to play a part in transforming it for the next generation has been an incredibly emotional journey,” she said.

She thanked councillors Faisal Rana and Amber Nisa, Rochdale Borough Council and its Environmental Management Team, alongside everyone involved in bringing the project forward.

Mrs Faisal said the improvements were about investing in children and creating a space where families could make memories together.

“From playing in Falinge Park as a child to helping shape its future, this really is a full-circle moment,” she added.

The announcement refers to a hoped-for start towards the end of February, with work continuing into March, subject to final arrangements. It does not specify the year or confirm an opening date, so that timetable remains to be clarified.

Residents have been invited to share their views on the proposals.

articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council will host three free firework displays across the borough in early November, featuring reduced noise fireworks for accessibility.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has confirmed a series of free firework displays to celebrate Bonfire Night in November 2026. The events will take place at three locations across the borough, including Middleton, Heywood, and Syke, with festivities beginning on Monday, November 2.

The first event will be held at Bowlee Community Park, located on Heywood Old Road in Middleton, starting at 6pm. The bonfire will be lit at 7pm, followed by fireworks at 7.30pm. The second display will occur on Tuesday, November 3, at Queen’s Park Road in Heywood, with the same timings. The final council-run event will take place on Thursday, November 4, at Cronkeyshaw Common in Syke, also starting at 6pm.

In addition to the council events, Milnrow Cricket Club and Lobden Golf Club in Whitworth will host their own firework displays on Saturday, November 7. The Milnrow event will charge £7 for adults and £11.25 for families, while the Lobden Golf Club display will cost £5 for adults and £3 for children.

Rochdale Council has introduced reduced noise fireworks this year to make the displays more accessible for all attendees. The council advises visitors to walk or use public transport due to limited parking at the venues. articles.title: Did Robin Hood really come to Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: Local stories tie a lost ring, witches and a 'Fairy Chapel' to Robin Hood — the tales are colourful, but what do the records actually show?
articles.summary: Local stories tie a lost ring, witches and a 'Fairy Chapel' to Robin Hood — the tales are colourful, but what do the records actually show?
articles.body:
There is a pulpit-shaped rock, a narrow pool and a name — the Fairy Chapel — at the base of Healey Dell’s steep gorge. The visitor centre and local heritage guides record a set of vivid stories: a King of the Fairies who turned a coven to stone, a ring lost in the river that cost a would‑be heir his title, and an origin tale that sends “Robert of Huntingdon” on the road to becoming Robin Hood. These versions are the ones you’ll see on site interpretation and in the Heritage Centre’s write‑ups. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

That is folklore, not archival evidence. The most systematic scholarly account of the Dell is an archaeological desk‑based assessment carried out for Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council by the University of Manchester Archaeological Unit in December 2004. It maps the valley’s mills, lodges, railway viaduct and later Victorian and industrial remains; it lists the local archives and printed sources consulted (John Rylands, Lancashire Record Office, Rochdale Local Studies and others) and documents the Dell’s long industrial and landscape history — but it does not produce contemporary medieval records linking a historical Robin Hood or a Robert of Huntingdon to Healey Dell. Put bluntly: the detailed desk‑based study records place, industry and later antiquarian interest, not a medieval outlaw’s itinerary. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

Healey Dell’s real, verifiable past is useful and interesting in itself. The site is a designated local nature reserve and a managed visitor attraction, with a Victorian railway viaduct that is Grade II listed and the valley’s surviving mill archaeology. Rochdale Borough Council describes the reserve, the visitor centre’s pictorial displays and the family‑oriented Fairy Grotto as part of the attraction visitors can find at Dell Road, Healey. The viaduct and the visible industrial remains are the kinds of things that the archaeological assessment and Historic England record in statutory listings. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

How did the Robin Hood story arrive here? Local legends often accrete around striking landscape features; caverns, pools and ravines attract tales of fairies, witches and enchanted tokens across Britain. The Healey Dell accounts appear in local storytelling and modern retellings by the Heritage Centre and local guides: they make no claim to derive from contemporary medieval documents but preserve a late tradition tying a Huntingdon name and a lost ring to the Chapel. Those popular accounts are part of the Dell’s cultural history and of local imaginative life — important for tourism and local identity — but they do not equal documentary proof. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

On the bigger question of Robin Hood’s historicity, mainstream scholarship treats Robin Hood as a legendary figure built from ballads and popular tales rather than a single, verifiable medieval person whose movements can be read off local court rolls. Modern reference works and folklorists stress the ballad tradition and its late medieval and post‑medieval formation; many local Robin Hood claims around England are later inventions, popular attributions or imaginative explanations for landscape oddities rather than recordable events. That does not make the stories worthless — it makes them folklore. ([books.google.com](https://books.google.com/books/about/Oxford_Dictionary_of_English_Folklore.html?hl=en&id=w2BMSAAACAAJ&output=html_text))

So what can a reader reasonably take away? If you mean “is there documentary, contemporary medieval evidence that Robin Hood or Robert of Huntingdon passed through Healey Dell?” the answer is: no such evidence has been produced in the local archival and archaeological surveys cited by the University of Manchester assessment and by the council’s heritage material. If you mean “are there stories that people tell about Robin Hood, witches and a magic ring here?” the answer is yes — they are recorded in local guides and on site interpretation, and they help make the place culturally lively. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

If you want to read more or check sources yourself: the University of Manchester archaeological desk‑based assessment (2004) is the most thorough published study of Healey Dell’s historic fabric; Rochdale Borough Council holds the reserve’s visitor information; the Healey Dell Heritage Centre publishes the Fairy Chapel story used in interpretation. None of these sources substitutes for a named medieval document placing Robin Hood in the Dell — and until such a record appears, the Robin Hood connection belongs to folklore rather than local history. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

articles.title: Safeguarding concerns, community costs and fireworks raised at Rochdale council meeting
articles.excerpt: Farooq Ahmed raised concerns about safeguarding powers, while Jordan Tarrant-Short questioned venue costs, fireworks, foster care and Warwick Mill at full council.
articles.content_html:
Concerns about the potential misuse of safeguarding powers, community venue charges and fireworks nuisance were raised during Rochdale’s full council meeting on Thursday, October 15.

Councillor Farooq Ahmed questioned how the council prevented staff from overstepping their authority, while Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short pressed cabinet members on issues including foster-carer recruitment, Warwick Mill and access to community facilities.

Councillors also rejected a proposal to rescind the council’s climate emergency commitments and backed motions concerning energy costs in new homes, protecting pubs and condemning attacks on places of worship.

Concern over safeguarding powers

Ahmed stressed that protecting vulnerable adults and children must come first, but questioned whether safeguarding procedures could sometimes harm the people they were intended to protect.

He said some officers could overstep their authority, leaving service users and families feeling victimised. He suggested the term safeguarding could be abused and asked how the council ensured staff did not misuse their powers.

Councillor Shah Wazir said safeguarding should protect and support people without causing avoidable distress. He outlined expectations around involving residents in decisions, providing advocacy where required and reviewing complaints and practice.

Responding to Ahmed’s supplementary question, Wazir invited him to provide specific incidents and promised they would be examined. The mayor also encouraged Ahmed to report his concerns.

The exchange raised concerns about potential misuse; it did not establish that misconduct had occurred in any particular case.

Community groups facing venue costs

Tarrant-Short said community organisations had contacted him about hire charges at facilities managed by Your Trust, warning that costs could make their activities financially unsustainable.

He told the meeting that a local dance group had reported being quoted £11,000 for one evening at Heywood Civic Centre. The booking requirements and an explanation of that reported quotation were not established during the exchange.

He asked whether protections, concessions or community pricing policies could prevent voluntary organisations being priced out.

Councillor Sue Smith said reduced rates or room-hire waivers could be available where appropriate, but charges also had to cover staffing, technical support and other operating costs.

She asked him to send details so officers could investigate. Smith said she had helped groups reduce charges, sometimes through changes to booking dates or times, but did not announce a new borough-wide pricing policy.

Fireworks and stronger safeguards

Tarrant-Short raised residents’ concerns about fireworks being used throughout the year, describing distress to families, vulnerable people and pets.

He asked what action the council and partner agencies were taking, then pressed for lobbying for stronger regulation and enforcement powers.

Councillor Tricia Ayrton acknowledged the concerns and said she had been speaking with partner agencies about a coordinated response.

She also said the council’s three community bonfire events would use reduced-noise fireworks, accompanied by music and lights. In response to his request for stronger national action, she encouraged councillors to raise concerns with their MPs.

Recruiting and retaining foster carers

Tarrant-Short asked how the council would increase the number of local foster carers and provide enough family placements for vulnerable children.

Councillor Rachel Massey outlined work through the Greater Manchester fostering recruitment hub, alongside specialist fostering, training and support. She identified particular needs for carers supporting teenagers, sibling groups and children with disabilities.

In a supplementary question, Tarrant-Short congratulated the children’s services team before asking what recruitment targets would replace retiring carers and increase overall capacity.

Massey said recruitment strategies and targets existed, while stressing the importance of finding the right home for each child. She did not give a numerical recruitment target in that exchange.

Warwick Mill and local investment

Tarrant-Short asked whether Warwick Mill would be acquired through compulsory purchase.

Council leader Neil Emmott said the council had negotiated an agreement with the owner and that cabinet had approved exercising an option to purchase following due diligence.

Asked why decisive intervention had taken so long, Emmott pointed to private ownership and previous unsuccessful redevelopment proposals, saying the council was now taking action.

Tarrant-Short also called for more community events in Rochdale South, including his Balderstone and Kirkholt ward.

Later, he asked whether a previously discussed highways review meeting had taken place. Scrutiny chair Councillor Tom Besford said no date had yet been arranged and promised to follow it up with him.

Pub protections and council votes

Tarrant-Short formally moved an amendment to the pub-protection motion, which councillors approved unanimously. The amended motion subsequently passed, supporting action over restrictive covenants that can prevent former pubs reopening.

Councillors unanimously supported motions on reducing energy costs in new homes and condemning attacks on places of worship.

A proposal to rescind the council’s climate emergency commitments was defeated.

Nneamaka is one of six finalists in the newly qualified adult social worker category. The shortlist recognises practitioners at the beginning of their careers, giving Rochdale a representative among those in contention for national recognition.

Gold and silver award recipients will be announced at the October reception.

articles.title: Pacific, Mangos and Empire until morning: remembering Rochdale’s strip
articles.excerpt: Box-dye red hair, Jägerbombs and taxi queues that lasted hours—remembering Rochdale’s strip, its familiar faces and the venues keeping the town alive today.
articles.content_html:
Box-dye red hair, Jägerbombs and taxi queues that lasted hours—Rochdale’s nightlife in the 2000s and early 2010s was a whole chapter of growing up. And places such as Empire are still helping the town make memories.

There was a time when a night out in Rochdale came with its own wardrobe, soundtrack and familiar faces.

Box-dye red hair. Chinos. Ed Hardy. The infamous Rihanna jumper. Outfits that, looking back, were remarkably close to business casual—worn with complete confidence for a night on the strip.

Rihanna and Eminem provided the soundtrack. Ordering a Jägerbomb felt like an event. Pacific, Mangos, Litten Tree and Empire were names woven into the weekend.

Between the bars, the dancefloors and the eventual search for a taxi, Rochdale felt wonderfully alive.

One former glass collector and barmaid remembers an incredible scene: heaving venues, wonderful bouncers and, in her experience, few fights. When the night finally ended, queues for taxis could mean waiting for hours into the early morning.

The people who made the strip

Ask someone about their old nights out and they might start with a club. Before long, they will be talking about a person.

A favourite barmaid. A reassuring face on the door. Someone you always bumped into, whether you had arranged to meet or not.

Among those familiar faces was the man affectionately known to revellers as “the gas man”, remembered sitting at the corner of the strip.

The former bar worker recalls people stopping to hug him and give him money. Despite the difficult circumstances she remembers him facing, he was a beloved presence, recognised and greeted with affection.

His circumstances were his own, and a nickname cannot tell his whole story. But the warmth with which he is remembered belongs in the history of those nights, alongside the music and the venues.

The strip’s character came from its people.

From the glass collector’s side of the dancefloor

Working through those nights meant seeing what customers sometimes missed.

Collecting glasses through a crowded room. Keeping the bar moving. Watching the door team manage another wave of arrivals while friends tried to find one another inside.

The former worker remembers the bouncers warmly. Her account offers a different perspective from the assumption that a busy nightlife scene must have been defined by trouble: what stays with her is how enjoyable it was, how few fights she encountered and how much life filled the town centre.

That is a personal recollection, rather than a claim that every night passed without incident. But it captures something worth preserving—the pleasure of working somewhere everyone wanted to be.

What happened to Pacific, Mangos and Litten Tree?

Pacific, at 8 South Parade, is now listed as closed. An archived council entry records a premises-licence suspension beginning in July 2013 for non-payment of an annual fee or levy. That record does not, by itself, establish the venue’s final trading date or the full reasons it closed.

Sources: https://licensing.rochdale.gov.uk/1/LicensingActPremises/Search/204/Detail?APP_ID=80078 and https://www.pubsgalore.co.uk/areas/rochdale-central/greater-manchester/

Mangos’ connection to a later venue remains visible in the paperwork. The council’s licensing record for Trinity retains conditions referring to the operating plan for Mango Bar at 3 King Street. The familiar address acquired another identity, although the sources reviewed do not establish the complete changeover story.

Source: https://licensing.rochdale.gov.uk/1/LicensingActPremises/Search/203/Detail?LIC_ID=6700

Litten Tree’s premises at 10 Fleece Street subsequently became Yates and are now Courtyard Rochdale. CAMRA records its reopening under the Courtyard name in March 2024. For former regulars, the sign has changed, but the address remains somewhere people can meet for a night out.

Source: https://camra.org.uk/pubs/courtyard-rochdale-rochdale-153361

Empire: the night that kept going

Then there was Empire.

In the former bar worker’s memories, it was the infamous destination where the night could stretch towards 6am. Leaving meant discovering that the early morning had arrived while everyone was still enjoying themselves.

Empire remains part of Rochdale’s nightlife today. Its presently advertised Friday and Saturday hours run until 4am, with live bands and performances central to its programme.

Source: https://empirerochdale.co.uk/

Its contribution extends beyond an ordinary weekend. The council’s 2026 Feel Good Festival programme included performances throughout the day at Empire, followed by a midnight DJ slot.

Source: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/rochdale-feel-good-festival/indoor-venues

That continuing activity deserves recognition. Venues such as Empire give people a reason to come into Rochdale, meet friends, hear music and spend an evening in their own town.

The old strip cannot be recreated exactly. Its customers have grown older; their wardrobes, responsibilities and stamina may have changed.

But the affection remains—for the songs, the people, the staff who looked after everyone and the nights nobody wanted to finish.

Rochdale’s next great night out needs people willing to make it happen. Empire and the town’s other active venues are keeping that possibility alive.

What do you remember about the strip? Pacific or Mangos? Litten Tree before Empire? The Rihanna jumper, the Jägerbombs or the seemingly endless taxi queue? Share your memories—and give a mention to the bar staff, glass collectors and door teams who made those nights special.

articles.title: 21 YEARS IN ENGLAND'S BOTTOM 100: Central Rochdale neighbourhood ranked 24th most deprived
articles.excerpt: Government figures show a part of Central Rochdale ranked among England's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods in every index since 2004. Where did regeneration funding go — and what can actually be proved about residents' outcomes?
articles.content_html:
ROCHDALE DAILY INVESTIGATION | 12 OCTOBER 2026

A small part of central Rochdale has been ranked among England's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods in every national assessment since 2004. In the latest official figures it is 24th out of 33,755 areas — and one of just three places in England to have remained in that bottom 100 across all six releases over 21 years.

The finding is not an opposition-party accusation or a campaign slogan. It appears in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government's English Indices of Deprivation 2025. Its code is E01005482, its statistical name Rochdale 010C, and it falls within the wider Central Rochdale and Mandale Park area.

Official sources: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, English Indices of Deprivation 2025 statistical release https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release; Government neighbourhood explorer https://deprivation.communities.gov.uk/about-your-neighbourhood/E01005482; Government research report https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-research-report

2004. 2007. 2010. 2015. 2019. 2025.

The government's researchers identified only three neighbourhoods that were among the 100 most deprived in every one of those six releases: Rochdale 010C, Middlesbrough 003F and Wirral 011C. The government's research report places the Rochdale neighbourhood within the middle-layer area known as Central Rochdale and Mandale Park.

This is not a description of the whole borough and not even of all Central Rochdale. A Lower-layer Super Output Area is a small census-based statistical area, typically home to around 1,500–1,600 people. The boundary of the LSOA matters when discussing local projects and spending. The Department for Education, for example, locates Whitehall Academy on Whitehall Street inside Rochdale 010C, confirming part of the geography, but the area cannot be equated simply with all of Mandale Park or Rochdale town centre.

Source: Department for Education establishment record for Whitehall Academy, LSOA Rochdale 010C https://get-information-schools.service.gov.uk/Establishments/Establishment/Details/151391

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRIVING THE RANKING?

The 2025 government neighbourhood explorer states that employment deprivation is among the area's most severe problems: fewer than 1% of English neighbourhoods rank as more employment deprived. Rochdale 010C also ranks as the most deprived neighbourhood within the borough for income, with higher-than-usual income deprivation affecting children and older people.

The national index measures seven different types of deprivation: income, employment, education, health, crime, barriers to housing and services, and the living environment. Income and employment carry the largest weights at 22.5% each. In other words, the central issue here is not whether a street looks attractive after regeneration; it is the resources and opportunities available to the people who live there.

Source: Government deprivation explorer https://deprivation.communities.gov.uk/about-your-neighbourhood/E01005482; methodology and domain weights https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release

DOES THIS PROVE THAT ROCHDALE HAS BECOME POORER?

No. The government explicitly warns that deprivation rankings describe RELATIVE circumstances. They do not, on their own, measure absolute changes in poverty, wages, health or household income. Boundaries and methods have changed; the 2025 index includes 55 indicators rather than 39 in 2019. Residents could have experienced improvements while their area's national relative position remained extremely poor.

But staying among the 100 most deprived on six separate occasions is nonetheless compelling evidence of persistent relative disadvantage. A serious assessment of whether interventions worked requires more than a new building or investment headline: longitudinal data on earnings, employment, child poverty, housing quality, health and skills, combined with a clear account of which projects actually reached Rochdale 010C.

Source: Government statistical release and guidance https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release

THE REGENERATION MONEY: BIG HEADLINES, BUT WHICH STREETS?

In a 2023 article, Labour council leader Neil Emmott described a £400 million Rochdale town-centre investment programme, including projects such as Riverside, Upperbanks and the restored Town Hall. The council also says the town secured £23.6 million from the government's Towns Fund, intended to support regeneration, skills and connectivity over a wider geographic area. These are genuine funding and development announcements.

Yet neither £400 million nor £23.6 million is an audited total spent exclusively within Rochdale 010C. The figures include a range of projects, investment types, funding sources and locations. Treating either sum as money spent on the approximately 1,600 residents of this one neighbourhood would be misleading.

Sources: Rochdale Council leader's 2023 regeneration statement https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-leaders-blog/investing-future-boroughs-regeneration-continues; council Towns Fund overview https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/business-licensing/towns-fund-money-help-us-improve-rochdale

One more closely relevant entry does appear in Rochdale's formal capital programme: the 2025/26 budget shows £450,000 in external grant funding scheduled for 'Towns Fund – New Homes Central Rochdale', described as land acquisition and remediation before homes are built by Rochdale Boroughwide Housing and private developers. An earlier programme showed £360,000 scheduled in 2023/24 for the similarly named project.

But these are BUDGET entries, not proof that either amount was actually spent. 'Central Rochdale' is also a broader project designation than LSOA Rochdale 010C. The missing link is a project-by-project ledger with actual expenditure, precise sites, housing completions and beneficiary outcomes.

Sources: Rochdale capital programme 2025/26 to 2029/30, 'Towns Fund – New Homes Central Rochdale' https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s112547/Append.%201%20for%20Capital%20Programme%20202526%20to%20202930.pdf; 2023/24 capital programme https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s94502/Append.%205%20for%20Budget%20Report%20202324.pdf

WHAT HAS BEEN DONE ABOUT POVERTY?

The council approved 'The Future We Deserve', its borough-wide 2024–2029 anti-poverty strategy, in March 2024. The authority described rising destitution and inequality as reasons for taking a long-term approach. From April 2026 it also began allocating around £5 million in government-backed Crisis and Resilience Fund support across the borough to assist residents facing emergencies, housing pressures and the cost of essentials.

Those programmes matter. They are also different in purpose from capital investment: emergency food and housing support can reduce immediate hardship, while regeneration may seek longer-term jobs and productivity. Neither a borough-wide budget nor a policy document establishes how many residents of Rochdale 010C received support or whether the area's underlying deprivation indicators improved.

Sources: March 2024 Cabinet decision approving anti-poverty strategy https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieIssueDetails.aspx?IId=55806&Opt=3; council Crisis and Resilience Fund https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/cost-living/crisis-resilience-fund

THE COUNCIL'S OWN RESPONSE TO SOCIAL MOBILITY CONCERNS

In a 2025 response to a social-mobility investigation, Rochdale Council acknowledged significant poverty, deprivation and inequality while pointing to improvements in town centres, education, employment opportunities and transport. It highlighted Rochdale Sixth Form College, Hopwood Hall College, the restored Town Hall and wider development proposals as assets that could improve opportunity.

These represent reasonable arguments for regeneration. But they are evidence of provision and investment, not by themselves proof that low-income residents in Rochdale 010C have entered stable, well-paid work or escaped hardship. This investigation has not obtained an LSOA-specific outcomes evaluation to test that claim.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council response to the Independent Commission on Social Mobility, 2025 https://socialmobility.independent-commission.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Rochdale-Borough-Council-response-to-Deep-dives_-a-local-perspective-on-social-mobility.docx.pdf

WHO SHOULD ANSWER?

Rochdale Council is Labour-controlled, led by Councillor Neil Emmott. The Central Rochdale ward is represented in October 2026 by Councillor Farooq Ahmed (Workers Party of Britain), Councillor Waqar Khan (Workers Party of Britain) and Councillor Sameena Zaheer (Labour and Co-operative), who also holds a Cabinet portfolio for Corporate, Governance and Transformation. The ward is a different boundary from the statistical neighbourhood and its current councillors did not all serve throughout the 21-year period.

These affiliations identify democratic responsibility and representation; the deprivation index does not establish misconduct, negligence or causation by any individual councillor or political party.

Sources: Council councillor directory https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=7214; https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=5385; Workers Party councillor directory https://www.workerspartygb.org/our_councillors; council control https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/councilmeetings

SEVEN QUESTIONS THAT DESERVE DOCUMENTED ANSWERS

1. Which completed, current and planned projects since 2004 have physically overlapped the boundary of LSOA E01005482?

2. For each project, how much public funding was approved, contracted and actually spent — separated from private investment and borough-wide allocations?

3. What proportion of jobs created or safeguarded under those programmes went to residents of this exact neighbourhood, and at what wages?

4. How have child income deprivation, employment deprivation, housing conditions and school attendance changed in absolute terms over time, not merely national rankings?

5. What specific measurable targets did the 2024–2029 Anti-Poverty Strategy set for the most deprived neighbourhoods, and how does Rochdale 010C perform against them?

6. What data will the council use to demonstrate that forthcoming developments are benefiting the people already living in this neighbourhood, rather than simply changing the appearance or population mix of nearby streets?

7. Will the council publish an independently auditable, geographically itemised account of 20 years of spending and outcomes, and allow residents to examine the results?

WHY IT MATTERS

Rochdale's new shops, college provision, housing developments, town-hall restoration and cultural attractions are visible and can produce genuine benefits. The government's latest deprivation statistics show a different and equally important side of local economic life: one neighbourhood has remained among England's most deprived in every national index for more than two decades.

That is not proof that £400 million was wasted. It is proof that the success of regeneration cannot be established from the value of construction projects alone. The ultimate test is whether residents gain lasting opportunities, better homes, improved health and higher disposable incomes.

Rochdale Daily is inviting the council, its regeneration agency, the ward councillors, relevant public bodies and local community organisations to provide a full geographic spending-and-outcomes breakdown and their responses to these findings. Corrections and right of reply can be sent to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.
